```{r setup}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(ggcircos)
library(ggplot2)
set.seed(42)
```

## What a chord diagram is here

Each node owns an arc of the circle. Each link owns a *slot* inside the arc of
every node it touches, and is drawn as a ribbon between its two slots. The arc
width is proportional to the number of links a node carries — not to the
value of those links — so a busy node gets a wide arc and its links fan out
inside it. The value belongs to the ribbon's colour, not its foot.

ggcircos computes all of that once, into a plain table:

```{r layout-table}
lay <- circos_layout(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust")
head(layout_nodes(lay))
```

Every geom in the package reads this table. None of them recompute it. That
one decision is what makes the rest of this vignette — and facets, scales and
legends — work the way they do in ggplot2.

## The thirty-second version

```{r hello, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "A chord diagram of the mtcars correlation matrix."}
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text()
```

Line by line:

- `ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust")` builds the layout from the matrix
  and returns a plain `ggplot` object. It draws nothing itself.
- `geom_chord(aes(fill = r))` draws one ribbon per link, filled by the
  correlation value `r` (a matrix is turned into links with columns `from`,
  `to`, `r`).
- `geom_node_arc()` draws the node ring just outside the circle of links.
- `geom_node_text()` puts the node labels outside the ring.

The legend appeared without being asked for, because `fill` is a normal
ggplot2 aesthetic.

## Ordering the nodes

The order of the arcs is the layout's only real degree of freedom. Three ways
to set it:

```{r order}
# 1. input order (the default)
ggcircos(cor(mtcars)) + geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) + geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

```{r order-hclust, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Nodes ordered by hierarchical clustering: correlated variables end up adjacent."}
# 2. hierarchical clustering of the matrix
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) + geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

```{r order-explicit, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "An explicit order vector: the strongest correlations are pulled together by hand."}
# 3. an explicit vector of node ids — it must list every node exactly once
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = c("mpg", "wt", "cyl", "disp", "hp", "drat",
                                "qsec", "vs", "am", "gear", "carb")) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) + geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

`order = "hclust"` clusters the matrix and lays the leaves out around the
circle. For a correlation matrix this is almost always what you want: the
blocks of variables that move together become adjacent arcs, and the ribbons
stop crossing the whole circle.

What the order actually changed, as data:

```{r order-diff}
a <- layout_nodes(circos_layout(cor(mtcars)))
b <- layout_nodes(circos_layout(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust"))
data.frame(input_order = paste(a$id, collapse = " "),
           hclust_order = paste(b$id, collapse = " "))
```

## Colouring by value

`aes(fill = r)` maps a continuous variable; any ggplot2 fill scale works, and
the legend is automatic:

```{r colour-continuous, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "A diverging scale: positive correlations warm, negative cool."}
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "white", high = "firebrick",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "r") +
  geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

A discrete mapping is just as ordinary:

```{r colour-discrete, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Ribbons coloured by sign, a factor-level fill."}
m <- cor(mtcars)
ggcircos(m, order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = ifelse(r > 0, "positive", "negative"))) +
  geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

One caveat worth knowing: a continuous fill is quantised into batches before
drawing (so a 500-link diagram is a few dozen grobs, not 500). Each batch
draws with one exact colour, at most 8/255 off any member. Visually
indistinguishable; bit-for-bit not identical.

## Letting the values drive the geometry

By default every node gets the same arc and every link the same share of it:
the layout only knows which nodes are connected, and the value shows up as
colour. That is the right picture when a link is a *relationship* and all
relationships count the same.

`circlize::chordDiagram()` does the opposite: a node's arc is proportional to
the weight it carries, and a link's width is proportional to its own value.
`weight =` switches ggcircos to that behaviour:

```{r weight, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "weight = r: node arcs and link widths now follow the correlations, as chordDiagram() does."}
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust", weight = r) +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = r)) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "grey95", high = "firebrick",
                       midpoint = 0, name = "r") +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text()
```

Read the difference off the ring: without `weight` every variable owns
`2*pi/11` of the circle; with it `cyl`, `disp` and `mpg` are wide and `am`,
`qsec` are thin, because that is how much correlation they carry. Negative
values count by magnitude, so a strong negative correlation is a wide link
too.

```{r weight-check}
nd <- layout_nodes(circos_layout(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust", weight = "r"))
round(setNames(nd$width / sum(nd$width), nd$id), 3)
```

`weight` names a column of the link table. A matrix supplies `r`; for a link
data frame pass whichever column holds the value, e.g.
`weight = "pident"` (or unquoted, `weight = pident`).

## Ribbons or curves

```{r line, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "type = \"line\": the same slots, drawn as curves."}
ggcircos(cor(mtcars), order = "hclust") +
  geom_chord(aes(colour = r), type = "line") +
  scale_colour_gradient2(low = "steelblue", mid = "grey80", high = "firebrick",
                         midpoint = 0) +
  geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

`type = "line"` keeps the slot geometry — each link still leaves its node at
its own slot — but draws a curve instead of a filled ribbon. With many links
it stays readable where ribbons turn into mud. `curvature` controls how far
the ribbon bulges toward the centre; the default `"auto"` scales it with the
angular distance between the two ends.

## Sectors

A sector is a group of nodes drawn with a wider gap around it — the way
circlize groups chromosomes. Pass a `nodes` table with an id column and a
column naming the sector, then point `sectors` at it:

```{r sectors, fig.width = 5.5, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Two sectors (ref / qry) with a wider gap between them."}
nodes <- data.frame(
  id = c(paste0("ref", 1:4), paste0("qry", 1:4)),
  genome = rep(c("ref", "qry"), each = 4)
)
links <- data.frame(
  from = c("ref1", "ref2", "ref3", "ref1"),
  to   = c("qry2", "qry3", "qry4", "qry4")
)
ggcircos(links, nodes = nodes, sectors = "genome") +
  geom_chord(aes(fill = from)) +
  geom_node_arc() +
  geom_node_text() +
  geom_sector_label()
```

`geom_sector_label()` labels the sector, not the node; it uses the
ring-contiguous run of each sector's nodes, which is why a sector that
straddles the start angle still gets one label at its middle.

## Other input shapes

A link table is the general form — a matrix is just a shortcut for one:

```{r links}
head(data.frame(from = "mpg", to = "wt", r = cor(mtcars)["mpg", "wt"]))
```

Graph objects work directly:

```{r igraph, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "An igraph object: the same layout machinery, fed from a graph.", eval = requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)}
g <- igraph::graph_from_data_frame(
  data.frame(from = c("a", "b", "c", "d"),
             to   = c("b", "c", "a", "a"),
             w    = c(3, 1, 2, 4))
)
ggcircos(g) + geom_chord(aes(fill = w)) + geom_node_arc() + geom_node_text()
```

`tidygraph::tbl_graph` works the same way. What the package reads natively is:
a square symmetric matrix, a data frame with `from`/`to`, an igraph or
tbl_graph object. Anything else becomes one of those three before the layout
sees it.

## Getting the layout back as data

The layout is not hidden inside the plot. `circos_layout()` returns it, and
the `layout_*()` accessors return plain data frames:

```{r layout-data}
lay <- circos_layout(cor(mtcars)[1:6, 1:6], order = "hclust")
layout_nodes(lay)
```

```{r layout-links}
head(layout_links(lay))
```

Every column the geoms use is there: `theta0`/`theta1` are the node's arc,
and a link's `theta0`/`theta1` are the two slots it occupies. You can filter
it, join it, or feed it to your own geoms:

```{r custom-geom, fig.width = 5, fig.height = 5, fig.cap = "A hand-drawn node ring: geom_segment() over the layout table, no package geoms."}
nd <- layout_nodes(lay)
ggplot(nd, aes(x = 1, y = theta0)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 1, xend = 1, y = theta0, yend = theta1), linewidth = 4) +
  coord_circos(limits = c(0, 2 * pi)) +
  theme_circos()
```

This is the whole point of the design: the layout is data, the geoms are
consumers, and you are allowed to be one too.

## What this does not do yet

- No angular (clock) axis: `geom_track_axis()` is a radial ruler.
- Self-loops (`from == to`) need `self_loops = TRUE`; by default they are
  dropped with a message. With it, they are drawn as loops folded toward the
  centre (see `vignette("from-circlize")`).
- The y (angle) scale is fixed to `[0, 2*pi]` by the layout. Replacing it
  breaks angles, and the coordinate warns when you do.
